Veḷudvāra Chapter: The Discourse on the Wheel-Turning Monarch (Cakkavattirājasutta)
The setting was at Sāvatthī.
There the Blessed One … [as before] … said this:
“Bhikkhus, even though a wheel-turning monarch exercises sovereignty, lordship, and rule over the four continents, yet—”
With the breakup of the body, after death, he is reborn in a good destination, in a heavenly world, into the company of the Tāvatiṃsa devas.
There, surrounded by a host of nymphs in the Nandana Grove, endowed and possessed of the fivefold divine sense-pleasures, he enjoys himself.
Yet, being unendowed with four qualities, he is not yet liberated.
He is not yet liberated from hell, not yet liberated from the animal realm, not yet liberated from the sphere of hungry ghosts, nor from the states of deprivation,
the bad destinations, and the lower realms. Yet, monks, even if a noble disciple subsists on mere morsels of alms-food and wears rag-robes,
if he is endowed with four qualities, he is nonetheless liberated from hell, liberated from the animal realm, and liberated [from the other states].
He is liberated from the realm of ghosts and from the states of deprivation, the evil destinations, and the lower worlds.
By what four?
Here, monks, the noble disciple is endowed with verified confidence in the Buddha: [text continues]

‘Such indeed is the Blessed One: worthy, perfectly enlightened, perfect in knowledge and conduct, sublime, knower of the worlds, incomparable leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, awakened, blessed.
He possesses unwavering confidence in the Dhamma:
‘The Dhamma is well-expounded by the Blessed One, directly visible, timeless, inviting one to come and see, leading onward, to be realized by the wise for themselves.’
He possesses unwavering confidence in the Saṅgha:
"The Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing well; the Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing uprightly; the Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing methodically;
the Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing correctly—that is to say, the four..."

‘There are these eight pairs of persons, these sixteen individual persons; this is the Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples that is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, the unsurpassed field of merit for the world.
He is endowed with the virtues dear to the noble ones—unbroken, untorn, unblemished, unmottled, freeing, praised by the wise, unadhered-to, and conducive to concentration.
“He possesses these four qualities.
And, monks, the acquisition of the four continents does not equal even a sixteenth part of the acquisition of these four qualities.
Thus was the first [sutta].

Veḷudvāra Chapter The Discourse on the Depth of the Holy Life At Sāvatthī. “Monks, this holy life is deep, hard to see, hard to understand, peaceful, sublime, beyond the sphere of mere reasoning, subtle, comprehensible only to the wise. It is difficult for those who have followed other teachers, who hold other views, who have other inclinations, who have been taught by others, to enter into this Dhamma and Discipline. Why is that? Because, monks, it has not been seen, heard, or understood by them in this way. “Suppose, monks, there were a great tree standing possessed of heartwood. A man would come along, desiring its heartwood, seeking its heartwood, searching for its heartwood. He would cut down the great tree at its base and, having cut it down, he would peel away the outer bark, thinking: ‘This is the heartwood. But he would not find the heartwood. Then, having peeled away the outer bark, he would cut away the inner bark, thinking: ‘This is the heartwood. But he would not find the heartwood. Then, having cut away the inner bark, he would cut away the softwood, thinking: ‘This is the heartwood. He would cut down the great tree at its base and, having cut it down, he would peel away the outer bark, thinking: ‘This is the heartwood. And he would not find the heartwood. Then, having peeled away the outer bark, he would cut away the inner bark, thinking: ‘This is the heartwood. And he would not find the heartwood. Then, having cut away the root, he would cut away the stump, thinking: ‘This is the heartwood. And he would not find the heartwood. Then, having cut away the stump, he would dig around the base of the tree, thinking: ‘This is the heartwood. And he would not find the heartwood. “Then, monks, an eighth man would come along, desiring its heartwood, seeking its heartwood, searching for its heartwood. He would cut down the great tree at its base and, having cut it down, he would peel away the outer bark, thinking: ‘This is the heartwood. And he would not find the heartwood. Then, having cut away the inner bark, he would cut away the softwood, thinking: ‘This is the heartwood. And he would not find the heartwood. Then, having dug around the base of the tree, he would dig up the soil, thinking: ‘This is the heartwood. And he would not find the heartwood. “Then
“Bhikkhus, possessing four qualities, a noble disciple is a stream-enterer, no longer subject to rebirth in the lower worlds, fixed in destiny, and bound for full enlightenment.
What are the four?
Here, bhikkhus, a noble disciple possesses unwavering confidence in the Buddha:”

‘Such indeed is the Blessed One: an arahant, perfectly enlightened, endowed with clear knowledge and conduct, sublime, knower of the worlds, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One.
[The same applies to] the Dhamma … and the Saṅgha … [and so forth].
“He is endowed with the virtues dear to the noble ones—unbroken, ... [as before] ... leading to concentration.
Endowed with these four qualities, monks, a noble disciple is a stream-enterer, no longer subject to rebirth in the lower worlds, fixed in destiny, and assured of full enlightenment.
Thus spoke the Blessed One.
Having said this, the Sugata, the Teacher, then spoke further:
“Those who possess faith and virtue,
And clarity born from seeing the Dhamma;”
They indeed arrive in due time at the bliss that is the depths of the holy life. Thus ends the second [sutta].

Saṁyutta Nikāya 55.3 (SN 55.3, PTS SN v 344) 1. Veḷudvāra Chapter The Discourse to the Lay Follower Dīghāvu At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Nādika in the brick hall. Then the lay follower Dīghāvu approached the Blessed One; having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, the Blessed One said this to him: “Dīghāvu, when a noble disciple possesses four things, he is one who has reached the ultimate conclusion, one for whom there is no further state of being here. What four? Here, Dīghāvu, a noble disciple possesses confirmed confidence in the Buddha thus: ‘The Blessed One is an arahant, perfectly enlightened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One. He possesses confirmed confidence in the Dhamma thus: ‘The Dhamma is well-expounded by the Blessed One, directly visible, immediate, inviting one to come and see, applicable, to be personally experienced by the wise. He possesses confirmed confidence in the Saṅgha thus: ‘The Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing the good way, practicing the straight way, practicing the true way, practicing the proper way; that is, the four pairs of persons, the eight types of individuals—this Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, the unsurpassed field of merit for the world. He possesses the virtues dear to the noble ones—virtues that are untorn, unrent, unblotched, unmottled, liberating, praised by the wise, not adhered to, leading to concentration. When a noble disciple possesses these four things, Dīghāvu, he is one who has reached the ultimate conclusion, one for whom there is no further state of being here.

Then the lay follower Dīghāvu rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, and keeping him on his right, departed. Not long after the lay follower Dīghāvu had left, the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus, this lay follower Dīghāvu has declared final knowledge thus: ‘I am one finished with hell, finished with the animal realm, finished with the domain of ghosts, finished with the plane of misery, the bad destinations, the nether world; I am a stream-enterer, no longer subject to [rebirth in] the lower world, fixed in destiny, heading for enlightenment. “Bhante, it is wonderful, bhante, it is marvelous, bhante! How the Venerable Dīghāvu has declared final knowledge thus: ‘I am one finished with hell... I am a stream-enterer, no longer subject to [rebirth in] the lower world, fixed in destiny, heading for enlightenment. “Bhikkhus, this lay follower Dīghāvu does not speak as he says because he has seen only a mere fraction of the Tathāgata’s qualities. Bhikkhus, the Tathāgata is even more excellent than that, far more excellent. And yet, bhikkhus, this lay follower Dīghāvu has declared final knowledge thus: ‘I am one finished with hell... I am a stream-enterer, no longer subject to [rebirth in] the lower world, fixed in destiny, heading for enlightenment. This is what the Blessed One said. Elated, those bhikkhus delighted in the Blessed One’s words. [End of] Saṁyutta Nikāya 55.3: The Discourse to the Lay Follower Dīghāvu.
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Feeding Place.
Now at that time the lay follower Dīghāvu was afflicted, suffering, and gravely ill.
Then the lay follower Dīghāvu addressed his father, the householder Jotika:
“Come, householder, go to the Blessed One; having approached him, pay homage with your head at the Blessed One’s feet in my name, saying:
‘Venerable sir, the lay follower Dīghāvu is afflicted, suffering, and gravely ill;
he pays homage with his head at the Blessed One’s feet.’”
“And speak thus:
‘It would be well, venerable sir, if the Blessed One, out of compassion, would visit the residence of the lay follower Dīghāvu.
“Very well, dear,” the householder Jotika replied to the lay follower Dīghāvu, and he went to where the Blessed One was.
He approached him; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side.
Sitting to one side, the householder Jotika said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, the lay follower Dīghāvu is afflicted, suffering, and gravely ill.”
Thus he pays homage at the Blessed One’s feet with his head and says this:
“It would be well, venerable sir, if the Blessed One, out of compassion, would go to the residence of the lay follower Dīghāvu.”
The Blessed One consented by remaining silent.
Then the Blessed One, having dressed and taken his bowl and robe, went to the residence of the lay follower Dīghāvu;
having arrived, he sat down on the prepared seat. Having sat down, the Blessed One said this to the lay follower Dīghāvu:
“I hope, Dīghāvu, that you are bearing up, that you are getting by. I hope that your painful feelings are subsiding and not increasing, and that their subsiding is apparent, not their increase?
“Venerable sir, I am not bearing up, I am not getting by. My painful feelings are severe; they are increasing and not subsiding, and their increase is apparent, not their subsiding.
“Therefore, Dīghāvu, you should train yourself thus:”
‘I shall be endowed with unwavering confidence in the Buddha:

“Indeed, that Blessed One is an arahant, perfectly enlightened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One.
[And] in the Dhamma …’ [and so on].
"In the Saṅgha...
[and so on] ...I shall be endowed with the virtues dear to the noble ones, unbroken... [and so on] ...conducive to concentration.
In this way, Dīghāvu, you should train yourself.
“Venerable sir, those four factors of stream-entry taught by the Blessed One are found in me, and I am seen to possess those qualities.

For I, venerable sir, am endowed with verified confidence in the Buddha: ‘Thus indeed is the Blessed One: worthy, perfectly enlightened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the worlds, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One. [I am endowed with verified confidence] in the Dhamma... [and so on].”
“In the Saṅgha … [and] endowed with the virtues dear to the noble ones, unbroken … [leading] to concentration.
“Therefore, Dīghāvu, being established in these four factors of stream-entry, you should further develop the six qualities that partake of true knowledge.

“Here, Dīghāvu, dwell contemplating impermanence in all conditioned phenomena; perceive suffering in what is impermanent, perceive non-self in what is suffering, and perceive abandonment, dispassion, and cessation.
“Thus, Dīghāvu, you should train yourself.
“Venerable sir, these six qualities conducive to true knowledge that have been taught by the Blessed One are found in me, and I am seen to be practicing those qualities.”
“Venerable sir, I dwell contemplating impermanence in all conditioned phenomena; I perceive suffering in what is impermanent, non-self in what is suffering, abandonment, dispassion, and cessation.
Yet, venerable sir, it occurs to me:
‘May this householder Jotika not fall into distress after my passing.’”
“Do not think thus, dear Dīghāvu.
Come now, dear Dīghāvu, attend closely to exactly what the Blessed One has said.
Then the Blessed One, having exhorted the lay follower Dīghāvu with this instruction, rose from his seat and departed.
Then, not long after the Blessed One had departed, the lay follower Dīghāvu passed away.
Then a number of bhikkhus approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, they sat down to one side. Sitting there, those bhikkhus said this to the Blessed One:
"Venerable sir, that lay follower named Dīghāvu, who was exhorted by the Blessed One with a brief exhortation, has passed away."
“What is his destination, what is his future state?
“Bhikkhus, the lay follower Dīghāvu was wise; he practiced in accordance with the Dhamma and did not trouble me with legal questions concerning the Dhamma.
Bhikkhus, with the complete destruction of the five lower fetters, the lay follower Dīghāvu is of spontaneous birth, destined there for final Nibbāna, no longer subject to return from that world.”
The Third [Discourse].

The First Sāriputta Sutta On one occasion the Venerable Sāriputta and the Venerable Ānanda were dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park.
Then, in the evening, the Venerable Ānanda emerged from seclusion... [and] as he was sitting to one side, the Venerable Ānanda said this to the Venerable Sāriputta:

“Friend Sāriputta, on account of possessing how many qualities has this generation been declared by the Blessed One to be stream-enterers, no longer subject to rebirth in the lower worlds, fixed in destiny, with enlightenment as their destination?

“Friend, it is on account of possessing four qualities that this generation has been declared by the Blessed One to be stream-enterers, no longer subject to rebirth in the lower worlds, fixed in destiny, with enlightenment as their destination.
Which four? [The four factors of stream-entry.]”
Here, friends, a noble disciple possesses unwavering confidence in the Buddha:

"Thus indeed is the Blessed One: [the Arahant, the perfectly enlightened one, accomplished in knowledge and conduct, the Well-Gone, the knower of the worlds, the unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, the teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One]. [He possesses unwavering confidence] in the Dhamma... [and so on].
"In the Saṅgha...
[and so on] ... he is endowed with the virtues dear to the noble ones, unbroken... [and so on] ... leading to concentration.

It is, friends, because of possessing these four qualities that this person has been declared by the Blessed One to be a stream-enterer, no longer subject to rebirth in the lower worlds, fixed in destiny, and bound for full enlightenment."

The Second Discourse to Sāriputta Then the Venerable Sāriputta approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. As the Venerable Sāriputta was sitting to one side, the Blessed One said this to him:
“Sāriputta, this is what is called ‘the factor of stream-entry, the factor of stream-entry.’”
“What, Sāriputta, is the factor for stream-entry?

“Venerable sir, association with superior persons is a factor for stream-entry; hearing the true Dhamma is a factor for stream-entry; careful attention is a factor for stream-entry; practice in accordance with the Dhamma is a factor for stream-entry.
“Excellent, excellent, Sāriputta!”

“Indeed, Sāriputta, association with superior persons is a factor of stream-entry; hearing the true Dhamma is a factor of stream-entry; careful attention is a factor of stream-entry; practice in accordance with the Dhamma is a factor of stream-entry.
For this, Sāriputta, is called ‘the stream, the stream.
What, Sāriputta, is that stream?”
“Venerable sir, this very Noble Eightfold Path is the stream; that is to say:
right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration.
“Excellent, excellent, Sāriputta!”
For this very Noble Eightfold Path, Sāriputta, is the stream; that is to say:
right view … [and so on] … right concentration.
It is in this sense, Sāriputta, that one is called “one who has entered the stream, one who has entered the stream.”
“Who, Sāriputta, is a stream-enterer?
“Venerable sir, whoever is endowed with this noble eightfold path is called a stream-enterer; such a venerable one is of such a name and such a clan.
“Excellent, excellent, Sāriputta!”
“Sāriputta, whoever is endowed with this Noble Eightfold Path is called a stream-enterer; such is this venerable one, of such a name and such a clan.
The fifth.

1. The Chapter on Bamboo Gate.
The Discourse to Thapati.
The setting was at Sāvatthī.
Now at that time, a number of bhikkhus were engaged in making robes for the Blessed One, thinking:
"When his robes are finished, at the end of the three months, the Blessed One will set out on tour.
At that same time, the overseers Isidatta and Purāṇa were staying at Sādhuka on some business.
The overseers Isidatta and Purāṇa heard:
“It is said that many bhikkhus are engaged in making robes for the Blessed One, thinking:
‘When his robes are finished, at the end of the three months, the Blessed One will set out on tour.’”
Then the superintendents Isidatta and Purāṇa stationed a man on the road, saying:
"When you, good man, see the Blessed One approaching—the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One—then inform us.
After standing there for two or three days, that man saw the Blessed One coming from afar.
Having seen him, he approached the two chief ministers, Isidatta and Purāṇa; having approached them, he said this to the two chief ministers, Isidatta and Purāṇa:
"Venerable sirs, here comes that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One.
Now is the time for you to do as you see fit."
Then the superintendents Isidatta and Purāṇa approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, they followed closely behind him.
Then the Blessed One, having stepped down from the road, approached a certain spot at the foot of a tree; having approached, he sat down on the prepared seat.
The superintendents Isidatta and Purāṇa, having paid homage to the Blessed One, sat down to one side.
As they were sitting to one side, the overseers Isidatta and Purāṇa said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, whenever we hear that the Blessed One will set out on a wandering tour among the Kosalans from Sāvatthī, at that time there arises in us a lack of gladness and dejection.”
‘The Blessed One will be far from us.

But when we hear, venerable sir, that the Blessed One has set out on a walking tour among the Kosalans from Sāvatthī, at that time there arises in us dissatisfaction and dejection: [thinking], ‘The Blessed One will be far from us.’”
“The Blessed One is far from us.

But when we hear, venerable sir, that the Blessed One will set out on a wandering tour among the Kosalans and the Mallans, at that time there arises in us a lack of gladness and dejection: [thinking], “The Blessed One is far from us.”
‘The Blessed One will be far from us.

But when we hear, venerable sir, that the Blessed One has set out on a wandering tour among the Kosalans and the Mallans, at that time there arises in us dissatisfaction and dejection: [thinking], ‘The Blessed One will be far from us.’”
“The Blessed One is far from us.

But when we hear, venerable sir, that the Blessed One will set out on tour among the Vajjis with the Mallas, at that time there arises in us dissatisfaction and dejection: [“The Blessed One is departing from us”].
‘The Blessed One will be far from us.

But when we hear, venerable sir, that the Blessed One has set out on tour among the Mallas and the Vajjis, at that time there arises in us dissatisfaction and dejection: [‘The Blessed One will be far from us.’]”
“The Blessed One is far from us.

But when we hear, venerable sir, that the Blessed One will set out on a wandering tour among the Kāsīs with the Vajjis, at that time there arises in us a lack of gladness and dejection: [“The Blessed One is far from us”].”
‘The Blessed One will be far from us.

But when we hear, venerable sir, that the Blessed One has set out on a walking tour among the Kāsīs from among the Vajjis, at that time there arises in us dissatisfaction and dejection: [thinking], ‘The Blessed One will be far from us.’”
“The Blessed One is far from us.
But when we hear, venerable sir,
that the Blessed One will set out on a wandering tour from Kāsī to Magadha, at that time there arises in us a lack of gladness and dejection:
‘The Blessed One will be far from us. But when we hear, venerable sir,
that the Blessed One has set out on tour from the Kāsīs toward the Māgadhas, at that time there arises in us no small measure of dissatisfaction and no small measure of dejection:
“The Blessed One is far from us.

But when we hear, venerable sir, that the Blessed One will set out on a walking tour from Magadha toward Kāsī, at that time there arises in us gladness and joy: [“The Blessed One is not far from us”].
‘The Blessed One will be near to us.

But when we hear, venerable sir, that the Blessed One has set out on tour from Magadha toward Kāsī, at that time there arises in us gladness and joy: [thinking], ‘The Blessed One will be near to us.’”
‘The Blessed One is near to us.

But when we hear, venerable sir, that the Blessed One will set out on a wandering tour from the Kāsīs to the Vajjis, at that time there arises in us gladness and joy: [thinking], ‘We shall see the Blessed One.’”
‘The Blessed One will be near to us.

But when we hear, venerable sir, that the Blessed One has set out on tour from Kāsī toward the Vajjis, at that time there arises in us gladness and joy: [thinking], ‘The Blessed One will be near to us.’”
“The Blessed One is near to us.

But when we hear, venerable sir, that the Blessed One will set out on tour among the Vajjis from among the Mallans, at that time there arises in us joy and gladness: [thinking], “We shall see the Blessed One.”
‘The Blessed One will be near to us.

Thus have I heard:

‘Such indeed is the Blessed One: worthy, perfectly enlightened, endowed with knowledge and conduct, sublime, knower of the worlds, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One.
Having realized this world—with its gods, Māras, and Brahmās, this generation with its recluses and brahmins, its princes and its people—by his own direct knowledge, he makes it known.

He teaches the Dhamma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing; he reveals the holy life in its entirety, perfectly complete and pure.
“It is indeed good to see such Arahants.
Then those brahmin householders of Veḷudvāra approached the Blessed One.
Having approached, some paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side; others exchanged greetings with the Blessed One.
They exchanged greetings; having concluded the polite and courteous conversation, they sat down to one side.
Some, having extended their joined palms toward the Blessed One, sat down to one side.
Some, having announced their name and clan in the presence of the Blessed One, sat down to one side. Some sat down to one side in silence.
As they were sitting to one side, those brahmin householders of Veḷudvāra said this to the Blessed One:
"Master Gotama, we have such desires, such inclinations, and such intentions:
'May we dwell in a bed crowded with children; may we enjoy Kāsī sandalwood; [may we enjoy] garlands, scents, and unguents...'"

"We would uphold [the training], we would accept gold and silver, and upon the breakup of the body, after death, we would be reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world. For us who have such desires,

“Teach us so that we might dwell upon a bed crowded with children... and be reborn in a happy destination, in a heavenly world.
“Householders, I shall teach you a discourse on the Dhamma concerning yourselves.
Listen to it and attend closely; I will speak.”

“And what, householders, is the Dhamma discourse concerning oneself?
In this case, householders, a noble disciple reflects thus:
‘I indeed desire to live, do not desire to die, desire happiness, and am averse to suffering.
If anyone were to deprive me—me who desires to live, does not desire to die, desires happiness, and is averse to suffering—of life, that would not be pleasing or agreeable to me.’

Since this state is unpleasant and disagreeable to me, how could I bind another with it?"
Having reflected thus, he himself abstains from taking life, he encourages others to abstain from taking life, and he speaks in praise of abstaining from taking life.
In this way, his bodily conduct is pure in three respects.
Furthermore, householders, a noble disciple reflects thus:
‘If someone were to take what is not given by way of theft, that would not be pleasing or agreeable to me.
And if I were to take what is not given by way of theft from another, that would also be unpleasing and disagreeable to the other.
This state which is unpleasing and disagreeable to me is also unpleasing and disagreeable to the other.’
‘This quality is displeasing and disagreeable to me; how could I yoke another to it?

Having reflected thus, he himself abstains from taking what is not given, encourages others in the abstinence from taking what is not given, and speaks in praise of abstaining from taking what is not given.
In this way, his bodily conduct is pure in three respects.
Furthermore, householders, a noble disciple reflects thus:
"If someone were to commit adultery with my wives, that would not be pleasing or agreeable to me.

‘This quality which is displeasing and disagreeable to me is also displeasing and disagreeable to another.

"If someone were to ruin my welfare through false speech, that would not be pleasing or agreeable to me."
"If I were to ruin another's welfare by means of false speech, that would be displeasing and disagreeable to the other as well.

In this way, his verbal conduct is purified in three respects.

"If someone were to address me with harsh speech, that would not be pleasing or agreeable to me.

"This Dhamma which has been taught by me...
[as before] ...in this way his verbal conduct is purified in three respects.

The Discourse to the Venerable Ānanda.
On one occasion the Venerable Ānanda and the Venerable Sāriputta were dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park.
Then, in the evening, the Venerable Sāriputta emerged from seclusion and approached the Venerable Ānanda; having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Venerable Ānanda.
Having exchanged polite and courteous greetings, he sat down to one side. Sitting there, the Venerable Sāriputta said this to the Venerable Ānanda:

“Friend Ānanda, by the abandoning of how many things and by reason of possessing how many things has the Blessed One declared that these people are stream-enterers, no longer subject to rebirth in the lower worlds, fixed in destiny, and bound for full enlightenment?”

“Friends, it is through the abandoning of four things and by reason of possessing four things that this generation has been declared by the Blessed One to be stream-enterers, no longer subject to rebirth in the lower worlds, fixed in destiny, with enlightenment as their final goal. Which four?
Friends, it is by reason of such lack of confidence in the Buddha as an unlearned worldling might possess that [one is not a stream-enterer].”
After the breakup of the body, after death, one who lacks such confirmed confidence in the Buddha is reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, or hell.

But, friends, the kind of confirmed confidence in the Buddha with which a learned noble disciple is endowed, by virtue of which, after the breakup of the body, after death, they are reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world—that kind of confirmed confidence in the Buddha is as follows:

"The Blessed One is such, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, sublime, knower of worlds, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One."
"Friends, that kind of lack of confidence in the Dhamma which possesses the uninstructed worldling such that,
with the breakup of the body, after death, he is reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, or hell— that kind of lack of confidence in the Dhamma does not exist in him.

And that kind of verified confidence in the Dhamma which possesses the instructed noble disciple such that, with the breakup of the body, after death, he is reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world— that kind of verified confidence in the Dhamma exists in him."
"The Dhamma has been well-expounded by the Blessed One...

[and] is to be realized by the wise for themselves. And, friend, that kind of lack of confidence in the Saṅgha which causes an unlearned worldling, upon the breakup of the body after death, to reappear in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, or hell—such a lack of confidence in the Saṅgha does not exist in him.

And, friends, it is with such unwavering confidence in the Saṅgha that a learned noble disciple, upon the breakup of the body, after death, is reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world—that kind of unwavering confidence in the Saṅgha he possesses:
"The Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing the good way... [and so on] ...it is the unsurpassed field of merit for the world."

"Friends, the kind of immorality with which an uninstructed worldling is endowed, such that upon the breakup of the body, after death, he reappears in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, or in hell— that kind of immorality does not exist for him. And friends,
the kind of virtue dear to the noble ones with which an instructed noble disciple is endowed,
such that upon the breakup of the body, after death, he reappears in a good destination, a heavenly world— that kind of virtue dear to the noble ones [does not exist for him]."
“They are unbroken... [and so on] ...conducive to concentration.

It is, friends, because of the abandoning of these four things and because of the possession of these four things that this generation has been declared by the Blessed One to be stream-enterers, no longer subject to rebirth in the lower worlds, fixed in destiny, with enlightenment as their destination.”

Saṁyutta Nikāya 55.17 (SN 55.17, PTS SN v 365) 2. Rājakārāmavagga Second Discourse on Friends and Companions At Sāvatthī. “Monks, there are these four kinds of friends and companions. What four? The friend who is a companion in misfortune, the friend who is a companion in prosperity, the friend who is a kinsman by blood, and the friend who is a virtuous person. These, monks, are the four kinds of friends and companions. “Monks, there are these four kinds of friends and companions. What four? The friend who is a companion in misfortune, the friend who is a companion in prosperity, the friend who is a kinsman by blood, and the friend who is a virtuous person. (1) “And what, monks, is the friend who is a companion in misfortune? Here, monks, when a friend falls into misfortune, whether it be the loss of relatives, wealth, or health, that friend does not abandon him; he stands firm for him, provides assistance, and does not turn his back on him. This is called the friend who is a companion in misfortune. (2) “And what is the friend who is a companion in prosperity? Here, monks, when a friend attains prosperity—whether it be the gain of relatives, wealth, or health—that friend does not become arrogant because of it; he shares in that prosperity, does not look down upon him, and does not treat him with contempt. This is called the friend who is a companion in prosperity. (3) “And what is the friend who is a kinsman by blood? Here, monks, whatever kind of duty one’s kinsmen have to perform, that friend performs it for them; and whatever kind of duty they have to perform for him, he performs that for them as well. He thinks: ‘I am their relative, and they are my relative. This is called the friend who is a kinsman by blood. (4) “And what is the friend who is a virtuous person? Here, monks, whatever kind of wholesome quality one possesses, such as faith, virtue, learning, generosity, or wisdom, that friend encourages one to cultivate them; he does not discourage one from them. He thinks: ‘May this good person develop these wholesome qualities even more. This is called the friend who is a virtuous person. These, monks, are the four kinds of friends and companions. When this was said, the Venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One: “It is wonderful, venerable sir! It is marvelous, venerable sir! How well this has been stated by the Blessed One: ‘The friend who is a companion in misfortune, the friend who is a companion in prosperity, the friend who is a kinsman by blood, and the friend who is a virtuous person. But, venerable sir, how is it that one comes to know: ‘This person is my friend who is a companion in misfortune’? And how is it that one comes to know: ‘This person is my friend who is a companion in prosperity’? And how is it that one comes to know: ‘This person is my friend who is a kinsman by blood’? And how is it that one comes to know: ‘This person is my friend who is a virtuous person’?

“Ānanda, when a person falls into misfortune—whether it be the loss of relatives, wealth, or health—and another person does not abandon him, but stands firm for him, provides assistance, and does not turn his back on him, then, Ānanda, one knows: ‘This person is my friend who is a companion in misfortune. When a person attains prosperity—whether it be the gain of relatives, wealth, or health—and another person does not become arrogant because of it, but shares in that prosperity, does not look down upon him, and does not treat him with contempt, then, Ānanda, one knows: ‘This person is my friend who is a companion in prosperity. When one sees that another person performs whatever kind of duty one’s kinsmen have to perform, and performs for them whatever kind of duty they have to perform for him, thinking: ‘I am their relative, and they are my relative,’ then, Ānanda, one knows: ‘This person is my friend who is a kinsman by blood. When one sees that another person encourages one to cultivate whatever kind of wholesome quality one possesses—such as faith, virtue, learning, generosity, or wisdom—and does not discourage one from them, thinking: ‘May this good person develop these wholesome qualities even more,’ then, Ānanda, one knows: ‘This person is my friend who is a virtuous person. “It is wonderful, venerable sir! It is marvelous, venerable sir! How well this has been stated by the Blessed One. And now, venerable sir, we understand: ‘This person is our friend who is a companion in misfortune’; ‘This person is our friend who is a companion in prosperity’; ‘This person is our friend who is a kinsman by blood’; and ‘This person is our friend who is a virtuous person. “Indeed, Ānanda, it is so. Indeed, Ānanda, it is so! Thus spoke the Blessed One. Delighted, the Venerable Ānanda rejoiced in the words of the Blessed One.
“Bhikkhus, those whom you might compassionately regard and who would think it worth listening to— whether friends, colleagues, kinsmen,
or blood relations— those, bhikkhus, should be encouraged, settled, and established in the four factors of stream-entry. Which four?”
They should be encouraged, established, and settled in verified confidence in the Buddha, [thinking]:
"Thus indeed is the Blessed One … [as above] … the Teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One.
Monks, there might be a change in the four great elements—the earth element, the water element, the fire element, and the air element.

Regarding the air element—it is simply not possible that there should be any alteration in a noble disciple who possesses verified confidence in the Buddha. Herein, what constitutes such an alteration?

That a noble disciple possessing verified confidence in the Buddha should be reborn in hell, or in the animal realm, or in the sphere of hungry ghosts—such a thing is impossible. Regarding the Dhamma … [and so on] … [regarding the Saṅgha …] … [regarding the training …] … [regarding the Ariyan virtues …] … it is simply not possible that there should be any alteration in a noble disciple who possesses verified confidence in the Ariyan virtues. Herein, what constitutes such an alteration? That a noble disciple possessing verified confidence in the Ariyan virtues should be reborn in hell, or in the animal realm, or in the sphere of hungry ghosts—such a thing is impossible.
In the Saṅgha...
[and so on] ... one should encourage, establish, and settle others in the virtues dear to the noble ones—virtues that are unbroken... [and so on] ... leading to concentration.

Monks, there might be a change in the four great elements—the earth element, the water element, the fire element, and the air element—but there could never be a change in a noble disciple who is endowed with the virtues dear to the noble ones.

In this regard, such a change of state would not be possible: that a noble disciple endowed with the virtues dear to the noble ones would be reborn in hell, in the animal realm, or in the sphere of hungry ghosts—this is impossible.

Monks, those whom you might feel compassion for, and who might think they should listen—whether friends, colleagues, kinsmen, or blood relatives—should, monks, be encouraged, established, and settled in these four factors of stream-entry.”

no longer subject to rebirth in the lower worlds, fixed in destiny, with enlightenment as his destination."
“Saraṇāni the Sakyan was one who did not fulfill the training.

Then Mahānāma the Sakyan approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, Mahānāma the Sakyan said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, here, Saraṇāni the Sakyan has passed away.”
Thus the Blessed One has declared:
"He is a stream-enterer, no longer subject to rebirth in the lower worlds, fixed in destiny, with enlightenment as his destination.
Thereupon, venerable sir, many Sakyans, having gathered and assembled together, grumbled, complained, and criticized [this]:
“It is wonderful indeed, sir! It is marvelous indeed, sir!
Who now would not become a stream-enterer here, when even Sakka Saraṇa has passed away?”
Thus the Blessed One declared:
“Saraṇāni the Sakyan is a stream-enterer, no longer subject to rebirth in the lower worlds, fixed in destiny, with enlightenment as his destination.
Yet, Saraṇāni the Sakyan was one who did not fulfill the training.’”
“Mahānāma, how could one who has long been a lay follower gone for refuge to the Buddha, gone for refuge to the Dhamma, and gone for refuge to the Saṅgha, go to a state of ruin?
For, Mahānāma, if anyone speaking rightly were to say of someone:
‘A lay follower who has long been gone for refuge to the Buddha, gone for refuge to the Dhamma, and gone for refuge to the Saṅgha,’ it is of Saraṇāni the Sakyan that one would be speaking rightly.”

"Saraṇāni, Mahānāma, Sakka has been a lay follower for a long time; he has gone for refuge to the Buddha, gone for refuge to the Dhamma, and gone for refuge to the Saṅgha. How could he go to a state of ruin?
Here, Mahānāma, a certain person is completely devoted to and full of confidence in the Buddha, thinking:
'Thus indeed is the Blessed One: ... [as above] ... the Teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One.'"
...in the Dhamma ...pe...
in the Saṅgha ...pe...
possessing laughter-like wisdom, swift wisdom, and endowed with liberation.

Thus, with the destruction of the taints, he dwells having realized for himself with direct knowledge in this very life the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, having entered upon it.

This person too, Mahānāma, is liberated from hell, liberated from the animal realm, liberated from the sphere of hungry ghosts, and liberated from states of deprivation, bad destinations, and perdition.
But here, Mahānāma, a certain person has gone to the Buddha for refuge and possesses absolute confidence—
"Thus indeed is the Blessed One … [as before] … the Teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One.
[Regarding] the Dhamma … [as before] … regarding the Saṅgha … [as before].
He possesses smiling wisdom and swift wisdom, yet he is not yet endowed with liberation.
Through the total destruction of the five lower fetters, he becomes one who attains nibbāna in the interval,
one who attains nibbāna upon landing, one who attains nibbāna without exertion, one who attains nibbāna with exertion, or one who goes upstream bound for the Akaniṭṭha realm.
This person too, Mahānāma, is liberated from hell, liberated from the animal realm, liberated from the sphere of hungry ghosts, and liberated from states of deprivation, ill destiny, and perdition.
But here, Mahānāma, a certain person has reached a definitive conclusion regarding the Buddha and is fully confident:
"Thus indeed is that Blessed One … [as before] … the Teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One."
[He is] not wise in the Dhamma... nor in the Saṅgha...
he is neither possessed of laughter-like wisdom, nor of swift wisdom, nor endowed with liberation.

Thus, with the complete destruction of three fetters and the attenuation of lust, hatred, and delusion, he becomes a once-returner; having returned to this world only once more, he makes an end of suffering.

This person, Mahānāma, is also liberated from hell, liberated from the animal realm, liberated from the sphere of hungry ghosts, and liberated from states of deprivation, bad destinations, and perdition.
Furthermore, Mahānāma, here a certain person has reached a state of absolute certainty and is full of confidence in the Buddha.
"Such indeed is the Blessed One … [as before] … the Teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One.
[The same regarding] the Dhamma … [as before] … and the Saṅgha … [as before].
He does not possess the wisdom of laughter, nor the wisdom of speed, nor is he endowed with liberation.
Yet, through the total destruction of the three fetters, he becomes a stream-enterer, no longer subject to rebirth in the lower worlds, fixed in destiny, and headed toward enlightenment.

This person too, Mahānāma, is completely freed from hell, freed from the animal realm, freed from the sphere of hungry ghosts, and freed from the states of deprivation, the bad destinations, and the lower worlds.
But here, Mahānāma, a certain person is not one who has gone for refuge with absolute certainty and full confidence in the Buddha...
nor in the Dhamma...
nor in the Saṅgha... [and so forth].
He does not possess the wisdom of laughter, nor the wisdom of speed, nor is he endowed with liberation;
nevertheless, these qualities are present in him:
the faculty of faith …pe… the faculty of wisdom.
And the teachings proclaimed by the Tathāgata are sufficiently accepted by his wisdom after careful reflection.

This person too, Mahānāma, is one who does not go to hell, does not go to the animal realm, does not go to the sphere of hungry ghosts, and does not go to the states of deprivation, the bad destinations, or the lower worlds.
But here, Mahānāma, there is a certain person who is not yet resolutely intent upon and fully confident in the Buddha...
He has no wisdom regarding the Dhamma …pe… no wisdom regarding the Saṅgha …pe… he possesses neither laughter-like wisdom nor swift wisdom, nor is he endowed with liberation.
Moreover, he possesses these qualities:
the faculty of faith … [and so on] … the faculty of wisdom.
And he has at least a measure of faith and a measure of affection toward the Tathāgata.

“Mahānāma, this person too is one who does not go to hell, does not go to the animal realm, does not go to the sphere of hungry ghosts, and does not go to the states of deprivation, the bad destination, or the lower world.

Mahānāma, suppose there were a field that was poor soil, a bad site, with unremoved stumps; and the seeds were broken, rotten, damaged by wind and sun, lacking essence, and poorly sown; and the rain-god did not send down a proper shower.

Would those seeds attain growth, increase, and abundance? “No, venerable sir. “In the same way, Mahānāma, this person is one who does not go to hell, does not go to the animal realm, does not go to the sphere of hungry ghosts, and does not go to the states of deprivation, the bad destination, or the lower world.”
“No, venerable sir. “In the same way, Mahānāma, here the Dhamma is poorly proclaimed, poorly expounded, not leading out, not conducive to peace, and not expounded by a Perfectly Enlightened One—
this, I say, is a field of suffering.”
And when a disciple dwells in that Dhamma, practicing in accordance with the Dhamma, practicing correctly, and living in conformity with the Dhamma—
I call this a bad seed. It is just as if, Mahānāma, there were a good field,
a well-prepared soil with the stumps well cleared away, and the seeds were unbroken, not rotten, not damaged by wind or heat, sound, and well-planted.
"And if the rain-god were to send down rain properly,
would those seeds attain growth, increase, and abundance?
"Yes, venerable sir."
“In the same way, Mahānāma, here the Dhamma is well-expounded, well-proclaimed, leading out, conducive to peace, and proclaimed by the Perfectly Enlightened One—
I call this a fertile field. And in that Dhamma,
a disciple dwells practicing in accordance with the Dhamma, practicing correctly, and living in conformity with the Dhamma.”
“I say that this one is a good seed;
how much more so, then, is Sakka Saraṇāni!
Mahānāma, at the time of his death, Sakka Saraṇāni was one who fulfilled the training.”
The Fifth.
Saṁyutta Nikāya 55.26 (SN 55.26, PTS SN v 380) 3.
Saraṇānivagga (The Chapter on Saraṇāni)
The First Discourse to Anāthapiṇḍika.
The setting was Sāvatthī.
Now at that time, the householder Anāthapiṇḍika was afflicted, suffering, and gravely ill.
Then the householder Anāthapiṇḍika addressed a certain man:
“Come, my good man, go to where the Venerable Sāriputta is; having approached him, pay homage with your head at the feet of the Venerable Sāriputta in my name, saying:
‘Venerable sir, the householder Anāthapiṇḍika is afflicted, suffering, and gravely ill.’”
“Thus he pays homage at the feet of the Venerable Sāriputta with his head.
And speak thus:
‘It would be well, venerable sir, if the Venerable Sāriputta would come to the residence of the householder Anāthapiṇḍika, out of compassion.’”
“Yes, venerable sir,” that man replied to the householder Anāthapiṇḍika.
He then approached the Venerable Sāriputta, paid homage to him, and sat down to one side.
Sitting there, he said this to the Venerable Sāriputta:
“Venerable sir, the householder Anāthapiṇḍika is afflicted, suffering, and gravely ill.
He pays homage with his head at the feet of the Venerable Sāriputta and says this:”
“It would be well, venerable sir, if the Venerable Sāriputta would visit the residence of the householder Anāthapiṇḍika out of compassion.
The Venerable Sāriputta consented by remaining silent.
Then, in the morning, the Venerable Sāriputta dressed, took his bowl and robe, and [went] together with the Venerable Ānanda...
With the attendant monk, he approached the residence of the householder Anāthapiṇḍika.
Having arrived, he sat down on the prepared seat. Once seated, the Venerable Sāriputta said this to the householder Anāthapiṇḍika:
"I hope it is bearable for you, householder; I hope you are getting by. I hope that painful feelings are subsiding and not increasing, and that their subsiding is apparent, not their increase?"
“Venerable sir, I am not getting better, I am not maintaining myself. My painful feelings are increasing, not subsiding; their increase is apparent, not their subsiding.

“Householder, you do not possess such lack of confidence in the Buddha as that which, when possessed by an uninstructed worldling, leads to reappearance in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, ruin, or hell, upon the breakup of the body after death. Such lack of confidence in the Buddha does not exist in you.”
Furthermore, householder, you possess unwavering confidence in the Buddha:
"Thus indeed is the Blessed One … [as above] … the Teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One.
As you recognize that unwavering confidence in the Buddha within yourself, your pain will subside right on the spot.
Householder, you do not possess that kind of lack of confidence in the Dhamma by which an uninstructed worldling,
with the breakup of the body, after death, is reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, or hell. Rather, householder,
you possess unwavering confidence in the Dhamma.
“The Dhamma has been well-expounded by the Blessed One … [and so on] … to be personally realized by the wise.
As you perceive within yourself that verified confidence in those teachings, feeling will subside immediately.
For, householder, with such lack of confidence in the Saṅgha as an uninstructed worldling possesses, when the body [breaks up]… [the unwholesome states increase].”
After death, one who has such lack of confidence in the Saṅgha is reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, even in hell.
But you, householder, possess unwavering confidence in the Saṅgha:
"The Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing the good way... it is the unsurpassed field of merit for the world."
Furthermore, as you perceive within yourself that unwavering confidence in the Saṅgha, your pain may subside on the spot.

Householder, the kind of immorality with which an uninstructed worldling—possessed of such immorality—is reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, or hell after the breakup of the body and after death: such immorality does not exist in you.
Indeed, householder, you possess the virtues dear to the Noble Ones... [which lead] to concentration.
Moreover, as you regard those virtues dear to the noble ones within yourself, your pain will be allayed on the spot.

Householder, that kind of wrong view possessed by the uninstructed worldling—which leads, with the breakup of the body after death, to rebirth in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, perdition, or hell—does not exist in you.
Indeed, householder, you possess right view.
Furthermore, as you regard that right view within yourself, your pain will immediately subside.

Householder, the unlearned worldling who possesses such wrong intention is reborn, with the breakup of the body after death, in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, or hell; yet you do not possess such wrong intention.
Moreover, householder, you possess right intention.
As you regard that right intention within yourself, your pain will immediately be allayed.

Householder, the kind of wrong speech with which an uninstructed worldling—upon the breakup of the body, after death—is reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, or hell—that kind of wrong speech does not exist for you.
Moreover, householder, you possess right speech.
If you were to regard that right speech as being within yourself, your pain would immediately subside.
For, householder, by such wrong action as the uninstructed worldling is possessed of regarding the body...
After death, one who possesses such wrong action of body would be reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, or hell;
yet you, householder, have no such wrong action of body. Indeed, you, householder, possess right action of body.
As you regard that right action of body within yourself, your pain would immediately be allayed.

"Householder, you do not possess that kind of wrong livelihood by which an uninstructed worldling, upon the breakup of the body after death, is reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, or hell.
Indeed, householder, you possess right livelihood.
And as you perceive that right livelihood within yourself, it is possible that your pain will be stilled."

“Householder, you do not possess that kind of wrong effort by which an uninstructed worldling, upon the breakup of the body after death, is reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, or hell.
But you do possess right effort, householder.
And as you regard that right effort within yourself, it is possible that your pain will subside.”

“Householder, that kind of wrong mindfulness with which the uninstructed worldling—upon the breakup of the body, after death—is reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, or hell, does not exist in you.
Indeed, householder, you possess right mindfulness.
And as you regard that right mindfulness within yourself, your pain will immediately subside.”
Householder, you do not possess that kind of wrong concentration by which an uninstructed worldling,
upon the breakup of the body after death, reappears in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm,
or hell; rather, householder, you possess right concentration.
Moreover, as you regard that right concentration within yourself, your pain will be allayed on the spot.

Householder, the kind of wrong knowledge possessed by the uninstructed worldling, through which—upon the breakup of the body, after death—they reappear in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, or hell—that kind of wrong knowledge is not present in you.
And yet, householder, you possess right knowledge.
Furthermore, if you regard that right knowledge as being within yourself, your pain would cease on the spot. Householder,
the unlearned worldling who possesses such wrong liberation as to be reborn in a state of deprivation,
a bad destination, a lower realm, or hell after the breakup of the body, after death— such wrong liberation does not exist for you.
“Householder, you do indeed possess right liberation.
As you regard that right liberation within yourself, your pain will immediately subside.
Then, at that very moment, Anāthapiṇḍika’s pains subsided.
Then the householder Anāthapiṇḍika served the Venerable Sāriputta and the Venerable Ānanda with his own rice-porridge.
When the householder Anāthapiṇḍika had seen that the Venerable Sāriputta had finished eating and had removed his hand from the bowl, he took a low seat and sat down to one side.
As the householder Anāthapiṇḍika was sitting there, the Venerable Sāriputta expressed his appreciation to him with these verses:
“He whose faith in the Tathāgata is unshakable and well-established,
and whose virtue is noble— ”
Beloved by the Noble Ones and praised.
Whoever has confidence in the Saṅgha and a vision that is upright;
They say that person is truly wealthy;
their life is not in vain.
Therefore, faith and virtue—
Confidence and the vision of Dhamma—
the wise person should devote themselves to these,
remembering the instruction of the Buddhas.
Then the Venerable Sāriputta, having expressed his appreciation to the householder Anāthapiṇḍika with these verses, rose from his seat and departed.

Then the Venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. As the Venerable Ānanda was sitting there, the Blessed One said this to him:
"Well now, Ānanda, where have you come from, arriving so late in the day?"
“Venerable sir, the householder Anāthapiṇḍika has been exhorted by the Venerable Sāriputta with this and that exhortation.
“Sāriputta is wise, Ānanda;
Sāriputta has great wisdom, Ānanda, in that he can analyze the four factors of stream-entry in ten ways!”
Sixth. Saṁyutta Nikāya 55.27 (SN 55.27, PTS SN v 385) 3.
Saraṇānivagga
The Second Discourse to Anāthapiṇḍika.
The setting was Sāvatthī.
Now at that time, the householder Anāthapiṇḍika was afflicted, suffering, and gravely ill.
Then the householder Anāthapiṇḍika addressed a certain man:
“Come, my good man, go to where the Venerable Ānanda is; having approached him, pay homage with your head at the feet of the Venerable Ānanda in my name, saying:
‘Venerable sir, the householder Anāthapiṇḍika is afflicted, suffering, and gravely ill.’”
“Thus he pays homage at the feet of the Venerable Ānanda with his head.
And speak thus:
‘It would be well, venerable sir, if the Venerable Ānanda would visit the residence of the householder Anāthapiṇḍika out of compassion.’”
“Yes, venerable sir,” that man replied to the householder Anāthapiṇḍika.
He then approached the Venerable Ānanda, paid homage to him, and sat down to one side.
Sitting there, he said this to the Venerable Ānanda:
“Venerable sir, the householder Anāthapiṇḍika is afflicted, suffering, and gravely ill.
He pays homage with his head at the feet of the Venerable Ānanda and says this:”
“It would be well, venerable sir, if the Venerable Ānanda would visit the residence of the householder Anāthapiṇḍika out of compassion.
The Venerable Ānanda consented by remaining silent.
Then, in the morning, the Venerable Ānanda dressed, took his bowl and robe, and went to where the householder Anāthapiṇḍika’s [residence was].
He approached the householder’s residence; having approached, he sat down on the prepared seat.
Once seated, the Venerable Ānanda said this to the householder Anāthapiṇḍika:
“I hope you are bearing up, householder; I hope you are getting by. I hope that your painful feelings are subsiding and not increasing, and that their subsiding is apparent, not their increase?”
“Venerable sir, I am not getting well; I am not enduring. My painful feelings are intense; they increase and do not subside. Their increase is apparent, not their subsiding.

“Householder, for an uninstructed worldling who possesses four qualities, there is trepidation, there is terror, and there is fear of death in the future. What are the four? [The Blessed One continued:]”
In this case, householder, an uninstructed worldling possesses lack of confidence in the Buddha.
When he perceives that lack of confidence in the Buddha within himself, he becomes terrified, he becomes agitated, and he experiences fear of death regarding the future life.
Furthermore, householder, an uninstructed worldling possesses lack of confidence in the Dhamma.
Furthermore, when he perceives within himself that lack of confidence in the Dhamma, he becomes terrified, he becomes agitated, and he experiences the fear of death regarding his future state.
Moreover, householder, the uninstructed worldling possesses a lack of confidence in the Saṅgha.
When he perceives within himself that lack of confidence in the Saṅgha, he becomes terrified, he becomes agitated, and he experiences the fear of death regarding his future state.
Furthermore, householder, the uninstructed worldling is possessed of immorality.
When he perceives that immorality within himself, there arises in him trepidation, there arises a state of paralysis, and there arises the fear of death regarding the future life.

It is because an uninstructed worldling is possessed of these four qualities, householder, that there arises in him trepidation, there arises a state of paralysis, and there arises the fear of death regarding the future life.
Householder, for a learned noble disciple endowed with four qualities, there is no trepidation, there is no paralysis, and there is no fear of death regarding the future life.
What are these four?
Here, householder, the learned noble disciple is endowed with unwavering confidence in the Buddha: [text continues]
"Such indeed is the Blessed One … [as before] … the Teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One.
Furthermore, when he perceives within himself this verified confidence in the Buddha, he has no trepidation, no consternation, and no fear of death regarding the future life.
Moreover, householder, the learned noble disciple possesses verified confidence in the Dhamma:
"The Dhamma has been well-proclaimed by the Blessed One... it is to be personally realized by the wise.
When he perceives within himself this confirmed confidence in the Dhamma, there is no fear, no trepidation, and no fear of death regarding the future life.
Furthermore, householder, the learned noble disciple possesses confirmed confidence in the Saṅgha:
“The Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing well … [and so on] … it is an unsurpassed field of merit for the world.
When he perceives within himself this verified confidence in the Saṅgha, he has no fear, no trepidation, and no fear of death regarding the future life.
Furthermore, householder, the learned noble disciple is endowed with the virtues dear to the noble ones—virtues that are unbroken … [and so on] … which lead to concentration.
And when he perceives those virtues dear to the noble ones within himself, he has no trepidation, no terror, and no fear of death regarding the future life.
Householder, for a learned noble disciple endowed with these four qualities, there is no trepidation, no terror, and no fear of death regarding the future life.
“Venerable Ānanda, I do not fear.”
Why should I be afraid?
For I, venerable sir, am endowed with verified confidence in the Buddha:
"Thus indeed is the Blessed One … [as above] … the Teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One."
I am endowed with unwavering confidence in the Dhamma …pe… and in the Saṅgha:
"The Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing the good way …pe… it is the unsurpassed field of merit for the world."
“Venerable sir, as for these training rules for laypeople that have been taught by the Blessed One, I do not see any breach of them in myself.
“It is a gain for you, householder! It is well-gained by you, householder!
You have declared, householder, the fruit of stream-entry.”
Seventh.
Saṁyutta Nikāya 55.28 (SN 55.28, PTS SN v 387) 3.
Saraṇānivagga
The Discourse on the Pacification of Fear and Terror.
The setting was at Sāvatthī.
As the householder Anāthapiṇḍika was sitting to one side, the Blessed One said this to him:
“Householder, when a noble disciple has stilled five fears and enmities,
possesses the four factors of stream-entry, and has well seen and well penetrated with wisdom the noble method,
he may, if he so desires, declare of himself:”

“I have exhausted hell; I have exhausted the animal womb; I have exhausted the realm of hungry ghosts; I have exhausted the states of deprivation, the evil destinations, and the lower realms. I am a stream-enterer, no longer subject to rebirth in the lower realms, fixed in destiny, and bound for full enlightenment.
Which five fears and enmities have been stilled?
Householder, one who destroys life generates fear and enmity pertaining to the present life, generates fear and enmity pertaining to future lives, and experiences mental pain and dejection.
For one who abstains from taking life, that fear and enmity is thus stilled.
As for one who takes what is not given, householder...
[and so on] ...as for one who engages in sexual misconduct, householder... [and so on].
Householder, when one speaks falsehood...

[and so on] ...householder, when one indulges in the use of fermented and distilled liquors that cause negligence, by reason of such indulgence in fermented and distilled liquors that cause negligence,
one produces fear and enmity both in this present life and in future lives, and produces mental distress.
One experiences suffering and mental distress.
For one who abstains from fermented and distilled liquors, which are the basis for negligence, that fear and enmity are thus stilled.
These five fears and enmities are stilled.
With which four factors of stream-entry is he endowed?
Here, householder, the noble disciple is endowed with verified confidence in the Buddha:
"Thus indeed is the Blessed One … the Teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One."
[He has faith] in the Dhamma …pe… in the Saṅgha …pe… he is endowed with the virtues dear to the noble ones, unbroken …pe… leading to concentration.
He is endowed with these four factors of stream-entry.
And what is his noble method that is well seen and well penetrated by wisdom?
Here, householder, the noble disciple attends thoroughly and wisely to dependent origination itself:
Thus, when this exists, that comes to be; with the arising of this, that arises.
Thus, when this does not exist, that does not come to be; with the cessation of this, that ceases. That is to say:
with ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise; with volitional formations as condition, consciousness arises... [and so on] ...
Thus is the origin of this entire mass of suffering.
But from the remainderless fading away and cessation of ignorance comes the cessation of volitional formations...
[and so on] ...thus is the cessation of this entire mass of suffering.
This noble method of his has been well seen and well penetrated by means of wisdom.
Householder, when these five fears and enmities have subsided for a noble disciple,
and he is endowed with these four factors of stream-entry, this noble method of his has been well seen by means of wisdom.
It has been thoroughly penetrated. If he so desires, he could declare of himself:

"I have exhausted hell; I have exhausted the animal realm; I have exhausted the sphere of hungry ghosts; I have exhausted the states of deprivation, the evil destinations, and the lower realms. I am a stream-enterer, no longer subject to rebirth in the lower worlds, fixed in destiny, and assured of full enlightenment.
This is the eighth [sutta].

Saṃyutta Nikāya 55.29 (SN 55.29, PTS SN v 389) 3. Saraṇānivagga Dutiyabhayaverūpasantasutta The Second Discourse on the Allaying of Fear and Dread “Bhikkhus, there are these five fears and perils that have not yet subsided for a clansman who has not gone forth. What five? The fear and peril of loss of relatives; the fear and peril of loss of wealth; the fear and peril of death; the fear and peril of states of deprivation; and the fear and peril of ill repute. These are the five fears and perils that have not yet subsided for a clansman who has not gone forth. But for one who has gone forth, bhikkhus, these five fears and perils have subsided. What five? The fear and peril of loss of relatives; the fear and peril of loss of wealth; the fear and peril of death; the fear and peril of states of deprivation; and the fear and peril of ill repute. These are the five fears and perils that have subsided for one who has gone forth.”
The setting was at Sāvatthī...
"Bhikkhus, when these five fears and enmities have been stilled for a noble disciple,
when he is endowed with these four factors of stream-entry, and when this noble method has been clearly seen by him through wisdom—
It has been well-penetrated. Desiring it, he could declare of himself:

"I have exhausted hell; I have exhausted the animal realm; I have exhausted the sphere of hungry ghosts; I have exhausted the states of deprivation, the evil destinations, and the lower realms. I am a stream-enterer, no longer subject to rebirth in the lower worlds, fixed in destiny, and assured of full enlightenment. Thus ends the ninth [discourse].

Saṃyutta Nikāya 55.30 (SN 55.30, PTS SN v 389) 3. Saraṇānivagga Nandakalicchavisutta At Sāvatthī. Then the Licchavi Nandaka approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, sat down to one side, and said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, it would be good if the Blessed One would teach me the Dhamma in brief, so that, having heard the Dhamma from the Blessed One, I might dwell alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute. “It is not easy, Nandaka, for one who has not seen for himself the nature of things to teach the Dhamma in brief. But since you have requested it, listen and attend closely; I will speak. “Yes, venerable sir,” the Licchavi Nandaka replied. The Blessed One said this: “Nandaka, there are these five aggregates subject to clinging. What five? The form aggregate subject to clinging, the feeling aggregate subject to clinging, the perception aggregate subject to clinging, the volitional formations aggregate subject to clinging, and the consciousness aggregate subject to clinging. These, Nandaka, are the five aggregates subject to clinging. Whatever ascetics or brahmins, Nandaka, regard these five aggregates subject to clinging as self or as belonging to self, they all regard these five aggregates subject to clinging in such a way. Why is that? Because, Nandaka, these five aggregates subject to clinging are what is meant by ‘self’ or ‘belonging to self’ for those ascetics and brahmins who regard them as such. Therefore, Nandaka, you should train yourself thus: ‘I shall not cling to the five aggregates subject to clinging. It is in this way, Nandaka, that you should train yourself. When this was said, the Licchavi Nandaka said to the Blessed One: “Magnificent, venerable sir! Magnificent, venerable sir!... From today let the Blessed One remember me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge for life. Then the Licchavi Nandaka, having delighted and rejoiced in the Blessed One’s words, rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, and keeping him on his right, departed. Not long after the Licchavi Nandaka had left, the Venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, sat down to one side, and said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, the Licchavi Nandaka has been converted; he has been won over by the Blessed One. “Ānanda, the Licchavi Nandaka is not yet fully converted. However, because of his faith, he will be reborn in a good destination, in a heavenly world. “But, venerable sir, how many people in the assembly of the Licchavis have been converted? “There are, Ānanda, some among the Licchavis who are stream-enterers, and others who are once-returners, and still others who are non-returners. “But, venerable sir, how many people in the assembly of the Licchavis have been won over? “There are, Ānanda, some among the Licchavis who have abandoned the five lower fetters, and others who have abandoned the five higher fetters. “But, venerable sir, how many people in the assembly of the Licchavis have been fully converted? “There is, Ānanda, only one person in the assembly of the Licchavis who has been fully converted. “But who is that person, venerable sir? “That is the Licchavi Nandaka, Ānanda. “Venerable sir, it is wonderful, it is marvelous! However, because of his faith, he will be reborn in a good destination, in a heavenly world. “Indeed, Ānanda, the Licchavi Nandaka is not yet fully converted; he is only half-converted. Bhikkhus, the Venerable Ānanda is capable of teaching the Dhamma to a group of bhikkhus, to a group of bhikkhunīs, to a group of male lay followers, or to a group of female lay followers. This is what the Blessed One said. Having said this, the Sublime One rose from his seat and went into his dwelling. Then, not long after the Blessed One had gone, the Venerable Ānanda addressed the bhikkhus: “Friends, bhikkhus! “Friend! those bhikkhus replied. The Venerable Ānanda said this: “Friends, it was in reference to this that the Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, when he rose from his seat and went into his dwelling after speaking these words, said: ‘Bhikkhus, the Venerable Ānanda is wise. He has understood the meaning of what was stated in brief by me. Bhikkhus, the Venerable Ānanda is capable of teaching the Dhamma to a group of bhikkhus, to a group of bhikkhunīs, to a group of male lay followers, or to a group of female lay followers. Then the bhikkhus, having understood the meaning of what was stated in brief by the Venerable Ānanda, taught the Dhamma to a group of bhikkhus, to a group of bhikkhunīs, to a group of male lay followers, and to a group of female lay followers. Saṁyutta Nikāya 55.31 (SN 55.31, PTS SN v 391) 4. Puññābhisanda Chapter (The Chapter on the Overflowing of Merit)

Setting at Sāvatthī.
“Bhikkhus, there are these four outpourings of merit, outpourings of the wholesome, nutriments of happiness.
Which four?

Saṃyutta Nikāya 55.34 (SN 55.34, PTS SN v 392) 4. Puññābhisanda Vagga Paṭhama-devapadasutta (The First Discourse on the Footprints of the Devas) “Monks, there are these four footprints of the devas. What four? First, monks, a noble disciple possesses confirmed confidence in the Buddha thus: ‘The Blessed One is an arahant, perfectly enlightened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One. Second, monks, a noble disciple possesses confirmed confidence in the Dhamma thus: ‘The Dhamma is well-expounded by the Blessed One, directly visible, immediate, inviting one to come and see, applicable, to be personally realized by the wise. Third, monks, a noble disciple possesses confirmed confidence in the Saṅgha thus: ‘The Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing the good way, practicing the straight way, practicing the true way, practicing the proper way; that is, the four pairs of persons, the eight types of individuals—this Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, the unsurpassed field of merit for the world. Fourth, monks, a noble disciple possesses the virtues dear to the noble ones—virtues that are untorn, unbroken, unspotted, unsplattered, liberating, praised by the wise, untarnished, leading to concentration. These, monks, are the four footprints of the devas.”
The setting was at Sāvatthī.
“Bhikkhus, there are these four divine footprints of the devas for the purification of beings who are unpurified, for the cleansing of beings who are uncleansed.
What are the four?
Here, monks, a noble disciple possesses unwavering confidence in the Buddha:
"Thus indeed is the Blessed One... the Teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One.
This is the first divine footprint of the gods for the purification of beings who are unpurified, for the cleansing of beings who are uncleansed.
Furthermore, monks, a noble disciple [possesses] confidence in the Dhamma …pe… in the Saṅgha …pe….
Furthermore, monks, a noble disciple is endowed with the virtues dear to the noble ones, unbroken …pe… leading to concentration.
This is the fourth divine footprint of the devas for the purification of beings who are unpurified, for the cleansing of beings who are uncleansed.
These, monks, are the four divine footprints of the devas for the purification of beings who are unpurified, for the cleansing of beings who are uncleansed.

Saṁyutta Nikāya 55.35 (SN 55.35, PTS SN v 393) 4. Puññābhisandavagga The Second Discourse on the Footprints of Devas At Sāvatthī. “Bhikkhus, there are these four footprints of devas. What four? ‘One who is intent on wholesome qualities is dear to us; one who is intent on unwholesome qualities is not dear to us. This is the first footprint of devas. ‘One who is intent on wholesome qualities is respected by us; one who is intent on unwholesome qualities is not respected by us. This is the second footprint of devas. ‘One who is intent on wholesome qualities is honored by us; one who is intent on unwholesome qualities is not honored by us. This is the third footprint of devas. ‘One who is intent on wholesome qualities is praised by us; one who is intent on unwholesome qualities is not praised by us. This is the fourth footprint of devas. These, bhikkhus, are the four footprints of devas. When this was said, a certain bhikkhu said to the Blessed One: “But how, Bhante, does one become intent on wholesome qualities, intent on unwholesome qualities? “Here, bhikkhu, one dwells with a mind obsessed by sensual lust, overwhelmed by sensual lust, and one does not understand as it really is the escape from the arisen sensual lust. This is called, bhikkhu, one who is intent on unwholesome qualities. Furthermore, bhikkhu, one dwells with a mind obsessed by ill will... obsessed by sloth and torpor... obsessed by restlessness and remorse... obsessed by doubt, overwhelmed by doubt, and one does not understand as it really is the escape from the arisen doubt. This too is called, bhikkhu, one who is intent on unwholesome qualities. Furthermore, bhikkhu, one dwells with a mind not obsessed by sensual lust, not overwhelmed by sensual lust, and one understands as it really is the escape from the arisen sensual lust. Furthermore, bhikkhu, one dwells with a mind not obsessed by ill will... not obsessed by sloth and torpor... not obsessed by restlessness and remorse... not obsessed by doubt, not overwhelmed by doubt, and one understands as it really is the escape from the arisen doubt. This too is called, bhikkhu, one who is intent on wholesome qualities. This is what the Blessed One said. Elated, that bhikkhu delighted in the Blessed One’s words. (This concludes the second discourse on the footprints of devas in the Chapter on the Overflowing of Merit.)
“Bhikkhus, there are these four divine footprints of the devas for the purification of beings who are impure, for the cleansing of beings who are uncleansed.

"Such indeed is the Blessed One—worthy, perfectly enlightened, endowed with knowledge and conduct, sublime, knower of worlds, incomparable leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One.

"Thus indeed is the Blessed One … [as above] … the Teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One."
