Saṃyutta Nikāya 55.37 (SN 55.37, PTS SN v 395) 4. The Chapter on the Outflow of Merit The Discourse to Mahānāma At Sāvatthī. There, the Blessed One said this to the venerable Mahānāma the Sakyan: “Mahānāma, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? The person who is intent on his own welfare but not on the welfare of others; the person who is intent on the welfare of others but not on his own welfare; the person who is intent neither on his own welfare nor on the welfare of others; and the person who is intent both on his own welfare and on the welfare of others. And how, Mahānāma, is a person one who is intent on his own welfare but not on the welfare of others? Here, Mahānāma, a certain person dwells having generated a mind of loving-kindness toward one direction, then a second, then a third, then a fourth—above, below, across, everywhere, and in all respects—extending the mind of loving-kindness, vast, exalted, immeasurable, and free from enmity and ill will. He dwells having generated a mind of compassion... a mind of sympathetic joy... a mind of equanimity toward one direction... [as above]... free from enmity and ill will. Yet he does not encourage others to dwell having generated a mind of loving-kindness... compassion... sympathetic joy... equanimity... free from enmity and ill will. It is in this way, Mahānāma, that a person is one who is intent on his own welfare but not on the welfare of others. And how, Mahānāma, is a person one who is intent on the welfare of others but not on his own welfare? Here, Mahānāma, a certain person encourages others to dwell having generated a mind of loving-kindness... compassion... sympathetic joy... equanimity... free from enmity and ill will. Yet he does not himself dwell having generated a mind of loving-kindness... compassion... sympathetic joy... equanimity... free from enmity and ill will. It is in this way, Mahānāma, that a person is one who is intent on the welfare of others but not on his own welfare. And how, Mahānāma, is a person one who is intent neither on his own welfare nor on the welfare of others? Here, Mahānāma, a certain person does not himself dwell having generated a mind of loving-kindness... compassion... sympathetic joy... equanimity... free from enmity and ill will, nor does he encourage others to dwell having generated a mind of loving-kindness... compassion... sympathetic joy... equanimity... free from enmity and ill will. It is in this way, Mahānāma, that a person is one who is intent neither on his own welfare nor on the welfare of others. And how, Mahānāma, is a person one who is intent both on his own welfare and on the welfare of others? Here, Mahānāma, a certain person himself dwells having generated a mind of loving-kindness toward one direction, then a second, then a third, then a fourth—above, below, across, everywhere, and in all respects—extending the mind of loving-kindness, vast, exalted, immeasurable, and free from enmity and ill will. He dwells having generated a mind of compassion... a mind of sympathetic joy... a mind of equanimity toward one direction... [as above]... free from enmity and ill will. And he encourages others to dwell having generated a mind of loving-kindness... compassion... sympathetic joy... equanimity... free from enmity and ill will. It is in this way, Mahānāma, that a person is one who is intent both on his own welfare and on the welfare of others. Of these four kinds of persons, Mahānāma, the person who is intent on his own welfare but not on the welfare of others is superior to the person who is intent neither on his own welfare nor on the welfare of others. The person who is intent on the welfare of others but not on his own welfare is superior to the person who is intent neither on his own welfare nor on the welfare of others. The person who is intent on his own welfare and on the welfare of others is superior to the person who is intent on his own welfare but not on the welfare of others, and is also superior to the person who is intent on the welfare of others but not on his own welfare. Of these four kinds of persons, Mahānāma, the person who is intent on his own welfare and on the welfare of others is declared the foremost, the best, the preeminent, the supreme, and the finest. Just as, Mahānāma, from a cow comes milk, from milk comes curd, from curd comes butter, from butter comes ghee, and from ghee comes cream-of-ghee, which is declared the foremost, the best, the preeminent, the supreme, and the finest among them—all these being derived from the cow—so too, Mahānāma, the person who is intent on his own welfare and on the welfare of others is declared the foremost, the best, the preeminent, the supreme, and the finest among these four kinds of persons.”
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling among the Sakyans at Kapilavatthu in the Nigrodha Park.

Then Mahānāma the Sakyan approached the Blessed One; having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, Mahānāma the Sakyan said this to the Blessed One:
“To what extent, Bhante, is one a lay follower?”
“Mahānāma, when one has gone for refuge to the Buddha, gone for refuge to the Dhamma, and gone for refuge to the Saṅgha—
to this extent, Mahānāma, one is a lay follower.
“But to what extent, Bhante, is a lay follower accomplished in virtue?”
“Mahānāma, when a lay follower abstains from taking life, abstains from taking what is not given,
abstains from sexual misconduct, abstains from false speech, and abstains from fermented and distilled liquors and intoxicants which are the basis for negligence—
to this extent, Mahānāma, a lay follower is accomplished in virtue.”
“But to what extent, venerable sir, is a lay follower accomplished in faith?
“In this case, Mahānāma, a lay follower is endowed with faith; he places faith in the awakening of the Tathāgata:
‘Thus indeed is that Blessed One … the Teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One.’”
“To this extent, Mahānāma, a lay follower is endowed with faith.
“But to what extent, Bhante, is a lay follower endowed with generosity?

“Here, Mahānāma, a lay follower dwells at home with a mind free from the stain of stinginess, open-handed, pure in hand, delighting in relinquishment, devoted to charity, and taking pleasure in distributing gifts.”
“In this way, Mahānāma, a lay follower is one who is accomplished in generosity.
“But in what way, Bhante, is a lay follower accomplished in wisdom?
“Here, Mahānāma, a lay follower is wise; he possesses the wisdom that discerns arising and passing away, which is noble, penetrative, and leads to the complete destruction of suffering.”
“In this way, Mahānāma, a lay follower is endowed with wisdom.
The seventh [discourse]. *Saṃyutta Nikāya* 55.38 (SN 55.38, PTS SN v 396).
4. The Chapter on the Overflowing of Merit;
The Discourse on Rain “Bhikkhus, just as when it is raining in thick drops upon a mountain peak above, that water flows down according to the slope...”
As it flows, it fills the mountain clefts, ravines, and gullies; the mountain clefts, ravines, and gullies being filled, fill the small pools;
the small pools being filled, fill the large pools; the large pools being filled, fill the small streams;
the small streams being filled, fill the great rivers; the great rivers being filled—

“...fill the great ocean; even so, bhikkhus, for a noble disciple, that which is unwavering confidence in the Buddha, that which is unwavering confidence in the Dhamma, that which is unwavering confidence in the Saṅgha, and those virtues dear to the noble ones— these qualities, flowing on,
lead to the further shore and result in the destruction of the taints.”
The Eighth.

"Godhā, a noble female disciple endowed with four qualities is a stream-enterer, no longer subject to rebirth in the lower worlds, fixed in destiny, and bound for full enlightenment.

When a noble disciple has abandoned these five lower fetters, he is one who attains final knowledge in this very life; or, if not, then with the abandoning of life, he becomes one of spontaneous birth, due to attain Nibbāna there without ever returning from that world. This, bhikkhus, is the fruit of once-returning for a noble disciple.”

Saṁyutta Nikāya 55.58 (SN 55.58, PTS SN v 411) 6. Sappaññavagga Arahattaphalasutta – The Fruit of Arhatship “Bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu is possessed of five qualities, he is capable of realizing the fruit of arhatship. What five? Here, a bhikkhu is possessed of faith, he places faith in the Tathāgata’s enlightenment thus: ‘The Blessed One is an arahant, perfectly enlightened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One. He is possessed of virtuous behavior; he dwells restrained with the restraint of the Pātimokkha, consummate in his behavior and sphere of activity, and having learned the rules, he trains by undertaking them. He is possessed of learning; he has learned much, retained what he has learned, and consolidated what he has learned. He recollects and reviews the teachings he has learned from the Teacher or his disciples. He is possessed of energy; he dwells with energy aroused for the abandoning of unwholesome states and the acquisition of wholesome states; he is steadfast, firm in exertion, not shirking the burden of wholesome qualities. He is possessed of wisdom; he possesses the wisdom that discerns arising and passing away, which is noble and penetrative, leading to the complete destruction of suffering. When a bhikkhu is possessed of these five qualities, he is capable of realizing the fruit of arhatship.”

Saṁyutta Nikāya 55.64 (SN 55.64, PTS SN v 412) 7. Mahāpaññavagga Vipulapaññāsutta (The Discourse on Vast Wisdom) “Bhikkhus, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? The person of vast wisdom; the person of quick wisdom; the person of moderate wisdom; and the person of sluggish wisdom. And how, bhikkhus, is one a person of vast wisdom? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu understands as it really is: ‘This is suffering’; he understands as it really is: ‘This is the origin of suffering’; he understands as it really is: ‘This is the cessation of suffering’; he understands as it really is: ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering. It is in this way, bhikkhus, that one is a person of vast wisdom. And how, bhikkhus, is one a person of quick wisdom? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu understands as it really is: ‘This is suffering’... ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering. He quickly penetrates that Dhamma with wisdom. It is in this way, bhikkhus, that one is a person of quick wisdom. And how, bhikkhus, is one a person of moderate wisdom? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu understands as it really is: ‘This is suffering’... ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering. He moderately penetrates that Dhamma with wisdom. Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu understands as it really is: ‘This is suffering’... ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering. He sluggishly penetrates that Dhamma with wisdom. It is in this way, bhikkhus, that one is a person of sluggish wisdom. These, bhikkhus, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world.”
